title: Paper Travels the World
summary: Paper went on a long trip! It traveled along the Silk Road to Samarkand and Baghdad, where it filled giant libraries, then across North Africa to Spain and Italy. Italian papermakers even learned to hide secret pictures called watermarks inside their paper.

sections.heading: Merchants, Caravans and a Bag of Lost Letters
paragraphs: In 1907, the explorer Aurel Stein was searching the ruins of an old Chinese watchtower in the desert west of Dunhuang, at the far western edge of China. In the rubble, he found a small bundle of letters, folded and tied, that had never been delivered. They were written on paper, in a language called Sogdian, and they dated to the early 300s CE. Today they are known as the Sogdian Ancient Letters.

The Sogdians were merchants from the region around Samarkand and Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan. They were the great traders of the Silk Road, the web of caravan routes that linked China with Central Asia, Persia, India and the Mediterranean. One of the letters was written by a woman named Miwnay, who had been left stranded in Dunhuang with her daughter and was furious with her husband for abandoning them. Another was a merchant's report about trouble in China. More than 1,600 years later, we can still read their worries, because they were written on paper.

Those letters tell us something important: paper was already traveling west in the hands of merchants hundreds of years before the Islamic world started making it. Silk Road towns such as Turfan, in today's western China, have also yielded many early paper documents. Paper moved the way most ideas moved on the Silk Road: slowly, from oasis to oasis, carried by traders, monks and travelers.

But carrying paper is not the same as knowing how to make it. For centuries, Central Asia and the lands further west mostly imported paper, or used other materials: papyrus in Egypt, parchment made from animal skin in the Mediterranean and Middle East, and even palm leaves and birch bark in India. The real turning point came when the skill of papermaking itself took root in the cities of Central Asia and the Islamic world.

sections.heading: The Battle of Talas and the Story of the Captured Papermakers
paragraphs: Our next stop is a battlefield. In the year 751, two great empires clashed near the Talas River, in a valley on the border of what are now Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. On one side was the army of Tang dynasty China, led by the general Gao Xianzhi. On the other side was the army of the Abbasid Caliphate, a vast Muslim empire that had just come to power in the Middle East, together with its allies. During the fighting, some of the Tang army's allies switched sides, and the Chinese army was badly defeated. Many Chinese soldiers were taken prisoner.

Here is where a famous story begins. According to a tradition recorded by later Arab writers, some of these prisoners were papermakers, and they taught their skill in Samarkand. From there, the story says, papermaking spread across the Islamic world. Samarkand did become famous for its paper; a writer in the 11th century, al-Tha'alibi, praised Samarkand paper and repeated the story about the Chinese captives.

It is a great tale, but historians treat it carefully, and you should too. It is a tradition, not a proven fact. Archaeologists have found evidence that paper was already present in Central Asia well before 751, and Sogdian merchants had been using it for centuries. Papermaking may have been practiced in the Samarkand region before the battle. Also, the writers who told the prisoner story lived long after the battle.

Interestingly, one of the Chinese captives, a man named Du Huan, actually wrote about his experiences. He was taken west and lived in the Abbasid lands for about ten years before returning to China by sea. In his account, he mentioned Chinese craftsmen he met there, including weavers, but he did not mention papermakers. That does not prove the story is false, but it is one more reason to be careful.

What we can say for sure is this: by the second half of the 700s, papermaking was well established in Samarkand and the cities of Central Asia, and over the next decades it spread to the heart of the Islamic world. One clever change happened along the way. The paper mulberry trees used in China did not grow well in these dry lands, so papermakers there relied on fibers they had plenty of: linen and hemp, often in the form of old rags and ropes. Rag paper would become the standard paper of the Islamic world and later of Europe for about a thousand years.

sections.heading: Baghdad: A City Built on Paper
paragraphs: In 762, the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded a new capital on the Tigris River: Baghdad. It was built as a perfectly round city, with the caliph's palace and great mosque at the center, and it grew quickly into one of the largest cities in the world. Merchants, scientists, poets and scholars came from everywhere.

Running an enormous empire, stretching from North Africa to Central Asia, took mountains of paperwork: tax records, letters, orders, maps and accounts. Around 794 to 795, during the reign of the famous caliph Harun al-Rashid, Baghdad began making its own paper. Later writers credited the powerful Barmakid family of government ministers with encouraging paper in government offices.

Why did officials prefer paper to parchment? One reason was cost: parchment had to be made from expensive animal skins, while paper could be made from cheap rags. Another reason, mentioned by later historians, was security. On parchment, a dishonest person could scrape off ink with a knife and write something new, and the change could be hard to spot. On paper, ink soaks into the fibers, so scraping it off leaves an obvious damaged patch. A government document on paper was harder to forge.

Baghdad's paper fed a whole new world of books. The city had a famous Paper Sellers' Market, the Suq al-Warraqin, lined with shops. A warraq was a person who dealt in paper and books: a stationer, copyist and bookseller all in one. Customers could buy fresh paper, order copies of books, or sit and read. A 9th-century geographer, al-Ya'qubi, wrote that Baghdad had more than a hundred booksellers' shops.

One of Baghdad's best-known writers, al-Jahiz, who lived from about 776 to 869, wrote an essay about the drawbacks of parchment, after a patron asked him to produce a book on it. He complained that parchment was heavy, swelled up when damp, smelled bad, cost too much and was easy to tamper with. He clearly preferred paper, which was lighter and easier to carry.

In Baghdad, scholars also worked on translating books from Greek, Persian and Indian languages into Arabic, including works of mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy by writers such as Aristotle, Euclid and Galen. This is often linked to the Bayt al-Hikma, the House of Wisdom, a library supported by the caliphs, especially Harun al-Rashid's son al-Ma'mun. Historians argue about how big or organized the House of Wisdom really was; some think it was mainly a palace library and translation office rather than a grand university. But everyone agrees that Baghdad became a world center of learning, and paper made it far cheaper to copy all those translations.

sections.heading: Cairo, North Africa and a Treasure Room of Scraps
paragraphs: From Iraq, papermaking spread west to Syria, where Damascus became an important paper center and trading hub, and then to Egypt. Egypt is a fascinating case, because it was the home of papyrus, the reed-based writing material that people there had used for thousands of years. You might expect Egyptians to stick with papyrus. Instead, paper slowly pushed papyrus aside, and by around the 900s and 1000s papyrus was falling out of use. Paper was simply more flexible, could be made from cheap rags, and did not depend on reeds growing in the Nile marshes.

Cairo grew into one of the great book cities of the medieval world. In the 1040s, a Persian traveler named Nasir-i Khusraw visited Cairo and was amazed to see that shopkeepers in the market wrapped the goods they sold, such as vegetables, spices and hardware, in paper. In most of the world at that time, paper was still too valuable to throw away like that. In Cairo it was common enough to use as wrapping.

Cairo also gives us one of the most astonishing paper treasure troves on Earth. In the Ben Ezra Synagogue in Fustat, the old part of Cairo, the Jewish community had a storeroom called a geniza. Jewish tradition said that writings containing the name of God should not be thrown away, so for many centuries people placed old papers there: letters, contracts, shopping lists, school exercises, prayers, medical prescriptions and much more. The dry Egyptian air preserved them. When scholars studied the Cairo Geniza in the late 1800s, they found hundreds of thousands of fragments, many of them on paper, giving an incredibly detailed picture of daily life around the Mediterranean in the Middle Ages.

Paper also changed mathematics. Earlier, calculations were often done on a dust board, a tray of sand where numbers could be drawn and quickly wiped out. With cheap paper, people could write out their calculations step by step and keep them. The Hindu-Arabic numerals we use today, the digits 0 to 9, spread through the Islamic world partly through books like those of the Baghdad mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose name gives us the word 'algorithm'. Paper helped these numbers travel.

Across North Africa, paper mills grew up in cities such as Fez in Morocco, which by the 1100s was an important papermaking center. Libraries grew enormous. Tales from the time describe the library of the Umayyad ruler al-Hakam II in Córdoba, Spain, in the 900s as holding hundreds of thousands of volumes. Historians think such numbers may be exaggerated, but even if the real count was smaller, these were some of the largest libraries in the world at the time, filled with books on paper.

One fair question is why the Islamic world, which loved paper and books so much, did not adopt printing for many centuries. Historians have suggested several reasons, including the great respect and beauty of handwritten Arabic calligraphy, especially for the Qur'an, the shapes of Arabic letters that join together in many forms, and the strength of a large, skilled copyist profession. We will meet the first Ottoman Turkish printing press much later in this Deep Dive.

sections.heading: Into Europe Through Spain and Sicily
paragraphs: Europe met paper through its southern doorways. Much of Spain, which Muslims called al-Andalus, was under Muslim rule for centuries, and the island of Sicily was ruled by Muslims in the 800s to 1000s before being conquered by Norman knights. Through these lands, paper and papermaking crossed into Europe.

Some of the oldest known documents on paper in Europe come from the Norman rulers of Sicily in the early 1100s. The paper itself was probably imported from the Islamic world, but it shows that European rulers were already using it.

The first big papermaking center on European soil was the town of Xàtiva (in Spanish, Játiva), near Valencia in eastern Spain. Around the middle of the 1100s, the geographer al-Idrisi wrote that Xàtiva made paper so good that it could not be found anywhere else in the civilized world, and that it was sent east and west. In 1244 the Christian king James I of Aragon conquered Xàtiva, but the papermakers, many of them Muslims, kept working, and the king's government used and taxed their paper.

Not everyone in Europe trusted the new material at first. In 1231, the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II, who ruled Sicily and southern Italy, ordered that official public documents should be written on parchment, not paper. He worried that paper would not last as long. For important legal documents that had to survive for centuries, many officials kept using parchment for a long time.

But paper had a huge advantage in price, and as Europe's towns grew, so did the need for cheap writing material. Merchants needed account books, notaries needed registers, students needed notebooks, and governments needed copies of letters. Around the 1100s, a French abbot, Peter the Venerable of Cluny, described books made from scraps of old rags, one of the first European mentions of rag paper. Papermaking spread from Spain into southern France by the late 1100s or 1200s. But the place that truly made European paper famous was a small town in the hills of central Italy.

sections.heading: Fabriano: The Town That Upgraded Paper
paragraphs: Fabriano sits in the Marche region of central Italy, in a green valley with fast streams running down from the Apennine Mountains. Papermills were set up there by the 1270s, and by the 1300s Fabriano was the most successful papermaking center in Europe. Its workers did not just copy the Islamic and Spanish methods. They improved them in three important ways.

The first upgrade was power. Beating rags into pulp by hand was slow, exhausting work. Fabriano's papermakers used waterwheels turned by the river to drive rows of heavy wooden hammers, often tipped with iron or nails, that rose and fell into troughs full of wet rags. These were called stampers. Several hammers worked side by side, pounding day and night as long as the water flowed. It was an early example of a machine doing factory work.

The second upgrade was sizing. Remember that paper fibers soak up ink like a sponge, and without sizing, ink spreads and blurs. Islamic papermakers had usually sized their paper with starch, often made from wheat or rice. Fabriano's makers used gelatin instead, a jelly-like glue made by boiling animal hides, hooves and bones. Each dried sheet was dipped into warm gelatin and dried again. Gelatin sizing made the paper stronger and smoother, gave a better surface for quill pens and European inks, and helped protect it from damage over time. Starch also attracted insects and mold, while gelatin did so less.

The third upgrade was the mould itself. Instead of screens made from bamboo or reeds, Italian makers built moulds with a screen of fine metal wires stretched across a wooden frame. Thin wires ran close together in one direction, held in place by thicker wires further apart in the other direction. That stiff wire screen made it possible for two workers to form sheets very quickly: one dipped moulds into the vat, while another flipped each fresh wet sheet onto a piece of felt. Stacks of sheets and felts were then squeezed in a big screw press to remove water.

Fabriano also used high-quality linen and hemp rags, and its river water was very pure. Modern scientists who have studied old Fabriano paper think its high calcium content and clean water help explain why so much of it is still in good condition today, more than 600 years later. Fabriano paper later supplied printers in Venice, Rome, Florence and Naples. Today the town has a Paper and Watermark Museum, where visitors can watch paper being made the old way. And the Fabriano company still makes paper, including some kinds used by artists.

sections.heading: Watermarks: Secret Pictures Inside the Paper
paragraphs: Fabriano's most famous invention was a hidden one. Try this: take a sheet of good writing paper or a banknote and hold it up to a bright window. You may see a faint picture or pattern glowing inside the paper. That is a watermark, and the earliest known European watermarks come from Italy, around 1282.

Here is how they work. Remember the wire screen on the mould. A papermaker would bend a piece of wire into a shape, such as a circle, a cross, a letter, a bull's head, a flower or a set of scales, and sew it onto the screen. When the mould was dipped into the vat, the pulp settled all across the screen, but where the wire shape stuck up, a little less pulp could settle. So the finished paper was slightly thinner along the lines of the wire design. Hold the sheet up to light, and those thinner areas let more light through, so the design glows.

If you look closely at old handmade paper against the light, you will also see faint lines across the whole sheet: many close-together lines and a few widely spaced ones. These come from the thin and thick wires of the mould screen. Experts call them laid lines and chain lines. Paper with this pattern is called laid paper.

Why did papermakers want watermarks? Mostly as a trademark, to show which mill made the paper and to advertise its quality. Watermarks could also show the size or grade of a sheet. Some historians point out that in Italy watermarks also helped show that paper was made locally rather than imported, which could matter for trade and church rules.

Watermarks turned out to be a gift to future historians. Each mould's wire design was slightly different, and moulds wore out and were replaced every year or two. So by comparing a watermark in an undated document with watermarks in dated documents, experts can often work out roughly when and where the paper was made. A Swiss scholar named Charles-Moïse Briquet spent decades collecting tracings of thousands of watermarks from European archives, and his great catalog, published in 1907, is still used today to date old papers and books, including early printed ones.

Watermarks can even reveal the secrets of famous books. When experts examined the paper copies of the Gutenberg Bible, which you will meet later in this Deep Dive, they found watermarks that helped show the paper had been imported over the Alps from northern Italy, probably from mills around Caselle in Piedmont. So the story of printing in Germany depended on paper made in Italian river valleys, using skills that had traveled all the way from China.

Watermarks are still with us. Many banknotes have a watermark portrait you can see against the light, because it is very hard to copy with an ordinary printer. A trick invented in medieval Italy is still helping to stop forgers today.

sections.heading: Mills Across Europe and a Hunger for Rags
paragraphs: From Italy, papermaking spread across Europe during the 1300s, usually carried by Italian craftsmen who were hired to set up new mills. A mill was established at Padua in 1340, and there were others around Bologna, Genoa and Venice. In France, more and more mills appeared, especially around Troyes in the northeast. In 1390 a Nuremberg merchant named Ulman Stromer founded one of the first paper mills in Germany, bringing in Italian workers to run it. He even made his workers swear to keep the methods secret.

England was slow to make its own paper and mostly bought it from abroad. Paper was in use there by the early 1300s, but the first known English papermaker, John Tate, did not start his mill near Hertford until the late 1400s.

All these mills had one big need: rags. European paper was made mostly from worn-out linen and cotton cloth, and it would stay that way until the 1800s. Rag collectors went from house to house and town to town, buying old shirts, sheets and sacks. The rags were sorted, cut into small pieces and left to soak and rot slightly in damp heaps, which loosened the fibers, before going under the stamping hammers. It was smelly work. In later centuries, rags became so valuable that some governments banned their export.

Linen had become much more common in Europe in the later Middle Ages, as people wore linen underclothes and used linen sheets. That meant more old linen for papermakers, and more paper. Over the 1300s and 1400s, paper became steadily cheaper than parchment. A sheep's skin could make only a few large sheets of parchment, but a mill could turn out thousands of sheets of paper from carts of rags.

Think how far paper had come. It had started as rough wrapping material and maps in Han dynasty China. It had traveled along the Silk Road in merchants' letter bags, been made in Samarkand and Baghdad, filled the libraries of Cairo and Córdoba, crossed into Spain and Sicily and been upgraded in Fabriano with waterwheels, gelatin and watermarks. By 1400, mills in Italy, France, Spain and Germany were turning out paper in large quantities.

Europe now had a cheap, smooth surface that was perfect for writing and, as it would turn out, perfect for printing. But in East Asia, people had already found a way to stamp whole pages onto paper at once.

deepDive: The westward journey of paper is a good case study in how historians separate stories from evidence. The Talas narrative, in which Chinese prisoners taken by Abbasid forces in 751 teach papermaking in Samarkand, appears in Arabic sources such as al-Tha'alibi (early 11th century), written roughly 250 years after the battle. Against it stands physical evidence: paper letters carried by Sogdian merchants in the early 4th century, early paper documents from Turfan and other Silk Road sites, and paper finds in Central Asia that predate 751. Historians such as Jonathan Bloom, in Paper Before Print (2001), argue that papermaking probably spread gradually through Central Asia, and that the more important event was the decision of the Abbasid state to adopt paper on a large scale in Baghdad from the 790s. In that view, the real driver was demand from a huge bureaucracy and a booming book trade, not a single group of captives. A second debate concerns materials and dating. Medieval European writers called Eastern paper charta bombycina or charta damascena, and for a long time scholars assumed it was cotton paper. Microscopic analysis has shown that most early Islamic and European papers were made mainly from linen and hemp rag fibers; 'damascena' probably reflects Damascus as a trading center. Dating European paper relies heavily on watermarks. The earliest known European watermarks date from about 1282 in Italy. Because a pair of moulds typically lasted only a year or two before wires bent or broke and were repaired, a watermark's exact shape can date paper quite closely. Charles-Moïse Briquet's Les Filigranes (1907) catalogued roughly 16,000 watermark tracings, and digital databases today extend his work. Finally, there is the question of why paper spread faster in Europe than parchment could be replaced in law. Rulers like Frederick II (1231) restricted paper for official documents because of doubts about durability. Ironically, good gelatin-sized rag paper from the medieval period often survives in better condition than the acidic wood-pulp paper made in the 1800s and 1900s, a problem this Deep Dive returns to later.
funFact: In the 1040s the Persian traveler Nasir-i Khusraw was amazed to see shopkeepers in Cairo wrapping vegetables and spices in paper, at a time when paper was still precious in most of the world.

check.q: How does a watermark become visible in a sheet of paper?
check.a: A wire design on the mould makes the paper slightly thinner there, so it shows when held up to light
wrong: It is painted on with invisible ink after the paper dries
It is pressed in with a hot iron stamp
It is printed with a special white ink
